newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian T-bills open stronger on tame U.S. data.
newsitem.headline: Canadian T-bills open stronger on tame U.S. data.

text.p: Canadian T-bills open stronger in active trade on Wednesday as tame U.S. economic data and a stronger currency helped send prices higher, dealers said.

"There wasn't much activity until those numbers came out. Now we're seeing positive reaction on both sides of the border," said one T-bill trader with a bank-owned brokerage. "Both these numbers people were looking at closely, the PPI and the retail sales."
Canada's three-month when-issued T-bill firmed to yield 3.18 percent from 3.24 percent at the close of trading on Tuesday.
Fixed-income markets in both countries strengthened after the U.S. Labor Department said the producer price index fell 0.1 percent in July, compared with expectations of a 0.1 percent rise.
Markets also benefitted from a report that U.S. retail sales rose 0.6 percent in July, below expectations of a 0.7 percent rise.
The reports helped the Canadian dollar rally below C$1.39 (US$0.7194), which benefited T-bills and dampened speculation of a near-term Bank of Canada rate hike.

The sharpest movement in the money market took place with the one year cash-T-bill, which weakened to yield 4.18 percent from 3.95 percent on Tuesday. Trading of the issue is being distorted by a major squeeze which came to light following yesterday's auction. Dealers said there is speculation a major U.S. player was responsible for the squeeze.

"My understanding is that the Bank of Canada of frowned pretty heavily on this and the situation seems to be correcting itself," said another dealer. "I would suggest that probably the Bank of Canada made a couple of phone calls. I think a little bit of moral suasion entered the scenario."
In other prices, the six-month when-issued T-bill firmed to yield 3.70 percent from 3.74 percent on Tuesday. The one-year when-issued T-bill firmed to yield 4.14 percent from 4.21 percent.
The call loan or overnight lending rate traded at 3.25 percent, the center of the Bank of Canada's 3.0-3.5 percent target range.
